transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Kansas is the next stop on President Trump's sprint across Republican strongholds with
just about two weeks left until the midterm elections.
As he was taking questions from reporters before he left the White House a short time
ago, Trump was asked if it was a bad sign for the GOP that he's going to campaign in
a state that voted for him.
He says his presence is a boost for Republican candidates.
My rallies are having a huge impact and a positive impact on the Republican Party.
I'm going to Kansas because I won it by a lot.
Trump is headed to a part of the country where farmers have been struggling to afford record
high diesel prices during the peak of harvest season.
Early voting began today in Texas.
Democrat James Tallarico is drawing on Texans' love of football as he tries to flip a Republican
Senate seat.
The Texas newsrooms police ganey reports.
Tallarico's "Clear Eyes, Full Hearts" tour borrows from Friday Night Lights, the TV
drama about Texas high school football.
It opened Sunday in Plano, a Dallas suburb in Republican-leaning Collin County.
President Trump carried that county by more than 11 percentage points in 2024.
University of Texas researcher Josh Blank says Tallarico needs votes beyond Democratic
strongholds.
The reality is as Democrats can win the urban and suburban parts of the state and still
lose the election if Republicans dominate the rural parts of Texas like they often do.
Tallarico faces Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Democrats haven't won statewide in Texas in more than 30 years.
For NPR News, I'm Blaise Ganey in Austin.
The midterms are on pace to be the most expensive election cycle on record.
More than $15 billion have been raised to influence who will win control of Congress.
That includes more than a quarter billion dollars in new spending by the world's wealthiest
person, Elon Musk.
Temporary protected status that was slated to expire today is being extended for people
from Ukraine and Sudan, although NPR's Jasmine Guards tells us it's unclear how long those
protections will remain in effect.
Temporary protected status or TPS grants temporary lawful residents work authorization and protection
from deportation to certain foreigners, tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of
Sudanese immigrants living in the U.S. have it.
In a statement, Homeland Security said a decision on both countries will be "made at the appropriate
time."
Until then, the agency added that Ukrainians and Sudanese who are enrolled in the program
will retain protection.
Over the last year and a half, the Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million
people from over a dozen countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti and Venezuela.
Jasmine Guards, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR News.
Artificial intelligence concerns are playing out beyond the United States.
Ireland is a tech hub in Europe, with Dublin home to the European headquarters of Meta,
Google and Microsoft.
Just last week, the Irish government hosted a conference touting ways that AI can make
Europe more competitive.
Meanwhile, as NPR's Willa Rubin tells us, a group of former tech workers and union organizers
staged a counter-summit to voice their AI concerns.
The thesis of this counter-summit can be summed up in a t-shirt worn by former tech worker
Bruno Bechistanicocelli. It's a picture of two people, all pixelated, smashing a computer.
And it says "Workers Against Slopaganda."
Slop, AI slop, and aganda, propaganda.
People here say AI is transforming the workplace so fast it could make jobs worse, replace
jobs, make people dumber.
They talk to solutions, like workers having a voice in management's decisions about how
and why they're using AI.
They're also suggesting a four-day work week.
The union is bringing these ideas to the next Irish parliamentary subcommittee meeting on
AI.
Willa Rubin, NPR News, Dublin.
Well, after more than four decades with CNN, Christiane Amanpour is leaving.
The network says its chief international anchor plans to depart CNN next June.
The 68-year-old Amanpour is also expected to end her PBS show Amanpour & Co. at the end
of the year, according to a statement shared by CNN.
However, Amanpour plans to keep her podcast The X-Files with her ex-husband, former diplomat
Jamie Rubin.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump campaigns in Kansas ahead of midterms, citing his strong rallies and past wins
Early voting begins in Texas; Democrat James Talarico courts voters in Republican-leaning Collin County
Midterm election spending on pace for record, with more than $15 billion raised including Elon Musk's spending
Trump administration extends temporary protected status for Ukrainians and Sudanese immigrants, with no end date set
Dublin counter-summit of former tech workers and unions voices concerns about AI in the workplace
Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN next June and end her PBS show Amanpour & Co. at year's end
